content.text:
I have everything I need. Let me now write the research note and submit the thesis.

---

## Company

Amer Sports owns Arc'teryx, Salomon, and Wilson — three premium sports and outdoor brands sold through its own stores, e-commerce, and wholesale. Revenue is product-driven across Technical Apparel, Outdoor Performance, and Ball & Racquet, with gross margins around 60% and an expanding direct-to-consumer channel.

## Bull Case

- **Clean beat on all three metrics, no one-time help.**
Q3 revenue grew 24% to $2.17B, with operating margin expanding over 70 basis points
adjusted EPS of $0.42 beat the $0.27 estimate by 55.6%, while adjusted net income rose 35% to $250M

. The beat came from real brand demand, not buybacks or tax items.

- **Guidance raised across revenue, margin, and EPS simultaneously.**
Amer lifted full-year revenue growth guidance to 25–26% and expects adjusted diluted EPS of $1.32–$1.35; its initial 2027 outlook calls for low-double-digit to mid-teens revenue growth.

This triple raise is exactly the signal that keeps institutional buyers adding through the drift window.

- **Arc'teryx and Salomon powering broad-based growth, not one brand carrying the other.**
D2C grew 36%; Technical Apparel revenue rose 26% to $861M led by Arc'teryx, while Outdoor Performance grew 27% to $917M driven by Salomon footwear and apparel, with D2C +48%.

Both businesses are accelerating at the same time.

- **Street is far above the current price — consensus target $46.86, low target $38, against a stock at $30.95.** [STRUCTURED: Analyst Coverage] Every analyst tracked is Bullish or Neutral, and
Cantor Fitzgerald maintained Overweight and raised its target to $47 on November 18.

The gap between the stock and even the most cautious sell-side target is 23%.

- **Store expansion runway still large.**
Management indicated the North American market could eventually support more than 200 Arc'teryx stores, up from the current 77 locations
, and
opened 9 net new Arc'teryx stores in Q3, on track for 30–35 for the full year.

Every new store is a D2C revenue stream that improves the margin mix.

## Bear Case

- **Stock is in a confirmed downtrend against the broader market.** [STRUCTURED: Price structure] The 50-day, 150-day, and 200-day averages are all falling, and the stock sits 27.6% below its 52-week high. This earnings gap is a bright spot inside a broken longer-term chart; if the gap fades, there is no technical floor from a healthy base. The tell: a close back below the gap-day low of $29.63.

- **Tariff exposure is real and not fully hedged.**
China-sourced goods sold into the U.S. account for roughly 10–12% of annual sales.
Some margin support in 2026 came from tariff refunds that will not repeat in future periods

— the underlying 2026 adjusted gross margin ex-refunds is 60.4% [STRUCTURED: earnings release]. Any escalation in U.S.–China tariffs hits Wilson specifically and pressures the margin guide. The tell: gross margin guidance revised lower at the Q4 report on Feb 22.

- **Wilson margin is already softening.**
Ball & Racquet Sports revenue grew 12%, but its adjusted operating margin narrowed 210 basis points to 6.1%.
The Ball & Racquet segment saw lower operating margin and a reduced full-year margin outlook.

If the weakness spreads to Arc'teryx or Salomon, the premium valuation (P/E 41) loses its support. The tell: Technical Apparel or Outdoor Performance margins declining in Q4.

- **ANTA Sports majority ownership is a governance overhang.**
The company remains controlled by China's ANTA Sports
with a dominant majority stake held by a small group of entities that limits minority shareholder oversight

. The $1B buyback was announced the same quarter — but minority holders cannot compel capital allocation decisions. The tell: related-party transactions rising, or buyback proceeds diverted, visible in quarterly filings.

- **Arc'teryx carries brand-concentration risk in China.**
A "Rising Dragon" controversy prompted Chinese authorities to mandate ecological compensation, and Arc'teryx's Greater China General Manager resigned — a critical growth market.
China and Europe remain uneven markets, and consumer demand could soften if economic conditions worsen.

A material decline in Greater China omni-comp (currently +16%) would surface first in Q4 commentary.

---

**Thesis check on the post's claim:** Volume cited as 2.7× — ground truth is 2.9×, same signal direction. EPS comparison used $0.35 estimate vs. ground truth $0.35–$0.36 (rounding); beat rate confirmed. All material claims hold. The gap day closed at $30.24 (their figure) — ground truth gap-day high $31.97, low $29.63; the Nov 18 close of $30.95 confirms the gap held on day 2, sitting above the gap midpoint of $30.80. Signal is clean.

**A note on the chart vs. the PEAD setup:** The Trend Template fails (1/8), meaning this stock is in a broad downtrend — the 50-day, 150-day, and 200-day averages are all falling. MA_PULLBACK requires a passing Trend Template, so that playbook is out. The gap day itself is the structure here: the PEAD watch triggers are written on the gap-day levels ($29.63 low, $30.80 mid), and the close today at $30.95 — above the midpoint — confirms the gap is holding on day 2. That is the buy signal the PEAD playbook asks for. The drift window is open until Feb 22. The market context (SPY below its 50-day) warrants awareness but doesn't disqualify a name-specific earnings catalyst.

**My one PEAD trade in the record is 0% wins, −1.3R over 15 days.** That's one trade — not a pattern — but I want to be honest that this setup demands I keep the floor tight. The gap-day low at $29.63 is the market's own line; a close below it ends the thesis.

**Conviction:** HIGH. This is a 4-for-4 serial beater with a triple raise (revenue, margin, EPS), a 24% growth rate, and a stock priced at $30.95 against a street-low target of $38. The gap held clean on day 2 on a down-market day. I am not going STRONG because the downtrend in the 150/200-day is real, the chart has no base, and the tariff/China governance tail is live.

input.core_belief: Amer Sports owns three premium sports brands — Arc'teryx, Salomon, and Wilson — that are growing double digits across every segment and geography, with direct-to-consumer expansion driving margin improvement. The business earns its premium multiple as long as Arc'teryx and Salomon continue to take share in technical outdoor and softgoods, and guidance raises keep institutional buyers adding. What must stay true: organic revenue growth stays above 20% and adjusted gross margin holds above 60% excluding non-recurring tariff refunds.

Adjusted gross margin (ex-tariff refunds) declines below 60% in the Q4 10-K or earnings release, indicating tariff headwinds or pricing pressure are compressing unit economics.
Arc'teryx Greater China omni-comp turns negative in Q4 commentary, confirming the brand-controversy risk is becoming a demand problem.
Technical Apparel or Outdoor Performance adjusted operating margin narrows by more than 150 basis points year-over-year in Q4, suggesting the high-margin D2C expansion is losing steam.
key_assumptions: Arc'teryx and Salomon combined revenue grows at least 20% in Q4 2026, confirming the momentum cited in the Q3 earnings call, checked at the Q4 report on Feb 22, 2027.
Adjusted gross margin (excluding one-time tariff refunds) holds above 60% in Q4 2026, confirming management's underlying 60.4% ex-refund guidance, checked in the Q4 earnings release on Feb 22, 2027.
Arc'teryx Greater China omni-comp stays positive in Q4, as a reversal there would indicate the brand controversy is accelerating, checked in the Q4 regional breakdown on Feb 22, 2027.
